sa.q: Define IoT and state the role of human intervention in it.
sa.a: IoT is the way of connecting physical objects through the Internet to other devices. It enables devices to talk to each other, collect data and make intelligent decisions with little or no human intervention — the automation of the decision step is what distinguishes IoT from a merely connected device.

sa.q: Why is the ATM considered significant in the evolution of IoT?
sa.a: The ATM (1974) allowed banking transactions outside banking hours, and is regarded as an early example of machine-to-machine (M2M) communication — a machine transacting with a bank's systems without a human intermediary.

sa.q: Distinguish between a sensor and a transducer.
sa.a: A transducer converts energy of one kind into another. "Transducer" is the collective term for both sensors (which sense energy forms such as movement, electrical signals, radiant, thermal or magnetic energy) and actuators (which switch voltages or currents). So every sensor is a transducer, but not every transducer is a sensor.

sa.q: Differentiate accuracy, precision and resolution with one example each.
sa.a:
Accuracy — closeness of a measurement to the true value. A sensor reading a 100 kg mass as 99.98 kg is 99.98% accurate (0.02% error).
Precision — reproducibility of repeated measurements. Applying exactly 150 mm Hg many times: a low-precision sensor's outputs vary considerably.
Resolution — smallest detectable change in the input. A sensor detecting 0.25°C changes has higher resolution than one detecting 0.5°C.

sa.q: Differentiate scalar and vector sensors.
sa.a: A scalar sensor produces an output proportional to the magnitude only of the measured quantity (temperature, pressure, colour, strain) — a thermometer responds irrespective of orientation. A vector sensor produces an output proportional to magnitude and direction (sound, image, velocity, acceleration) — an accelerometer gives components along x, y and z.

sa.q: What is aliasing error and what causes it?
sa.a: Aliasing error arises from dynamic error caused by mishandling of sampling frequencies. It causes different signals of varying frequencies to be represented as a single signal when the sampling frequency is not correctly chosen, so the input signal becomes a multiple of the sampling rate.

sa.q: What is virtual sensing? Why is it used?
sa.a: Virtual sensing uses real sensors for actual measurement and virtual sensors — estimated data points derived from those real measurements using mathematical models, correlations or extrapolation. It is used because (i) in large-scale deployments installing sensors everywhere is very costly and often unnecessary, and (ii) parameters such as soil moisture, temperature and humidity don't change drastically between neighbouring areas, so one field's readings represent nearby fields with little error.

sa.q: List the four sensing considerations for choosing a sensor.
sa.a: (1) Sensing range, (2) Accuracy & precision, (3) Energy, (4) Device size. The choice can "make or break the feasibility of an IoT deployment".

sa.q: Compare hydraulic and pneumatic actuators.
sa.a:
Hydraulic: uses a cylinder/fluid motor; because liquids are nearly incompressible it exerts considerable force and is a stiff, precise system; but it has limited acceleration (slow) and is heavy and bulky, unsuitable for portable IoT devices.
Pneumatic: converts vacuum or compressed air at high pressure into linear or rotary motion; produces large forces from relatively small pressure changes, responds quickly to start/stop signals, and its power source need not be stored in reserve.

sa.q: Why is correct actuator selection important?
sa.a: Actuators perform the heavy or mechanical tasks that carry out the physical action after sensing and processing. Correct selection matters for long-term reliability, operational efficiency and increased lifetime.

sa.q: Define a WSN and list any four of its features.
sa.a: A WSN is a network of spatially distributed sensors that monitor and record environmental conditions. Any four of: fault tolerance, scalability, long lifetime, security, programmability, affordability, heterogeneity, mobility.

sa.q: Name the four classes of WSN with one application each.
sa.a: WMSN (multimedia) — surveillance; UWSN (underwater, acoustic) — marine exploration; WUSN (underground) — pipeline fault detection; Wireless Mobile SN — vehicular sensor networks / traffic monitoring.

sa.q: Why do underwater sensor networks use acoustic communication?
sa.a: Nodes are deployed at various depths and communicate using acoustic waves, since radio propagation underwater is impractical. The consequences are the listed challenges: limited bandwidth, high latency and energy constraints.

sa.q: Define M2M and give two examples.
sa.a: M2M communication enables devices or machines to exchange data automatically without human involvement. Examples: ATMs notifying banks to refill cash; vending machines reporting low inventory; home power systems switching to generators during outages.

sa.q: List any four features of M2M.
sa.a: Negligible mobility; time-restricted transmissions; delay tolerant; packet-switched communication; small data footprint; event detection only; low power consumption. (Any four.)

sa.q: Distinguish low-end, mid-end and high-end M2M devices.
sa.a:
Low-end: inexpensive, basic sensing, power saving, no IP support, limited processing and range; deployed densely; used in environmental monitoring and agriculture.
Mid-end: costlier than low-end, less complex than high-end; may support mobility; localization, traffic control, TCP/IP, QoS; home automation, SCM, industrial automation, asset tracking.
High-end: expensive, high processing power, handles multimedia, ensures QoS even when mobile, mobility support standard; deployed sparsely; used in ITS, military and biomedical systems.

sa.q: Differentiate IP-based and non-IP-based M2M networks.
sa.a:
IP-based: supported by high-end devices; IPv4 and IPv6; communication with the IP network is direct, as both follow the same protocol structure.
Non-IP-based: supported by low- and mid-end devices; a separate addressing scheme accommodates these resource-constrained devices; the M2M area network forwards packets to the gateway, which packetizes them into IP packets.

sa.q: Define CPS and state its four defining characteristics.
sa.a: CPS are intelligent networked systems integrating sensing, computation, control and networking to interact with the physical world in real time. They (i) monitor and control physical processes through continuous feedback, (ii) work in an interdisciplinary domain (computing, mechanical, electrical, electronics, network engineering), (iii) involve human decision-making as part of the control cycle, enhancing reliability and adaptability.

sa.q: Explain the CPS feedback loop in steps.
sa.a: (1) Sensors collect environmental data → (2) data is sent over the network to a controller → (3) the controller processes it using intelligent algorithms → (4) actuators respond by changing the environment → (5) new sensor data is collected to see if the desired change occurred → (6) the loop continues until the system reaches its goal.

sa.q: Differentiate "interoperable" and "heterogeneous" as CPS features.
sa.a: Interoperable — integrates devices and software from different manufacturers so they work together. Heterogeneous — can handle different types of sensors, actuators, processors and software platforms.

sa.q: State two differences between IoT and M2M.
sa.a: (1) M2M covers interactions between machines and devices; IoT covers a broader range — device–device, thing–people, thing–application, people–application. (2) M2M was introduced by telecom service providers and emphasises telecom networks (3G/4G/5G, satellite); IoT includes Internet connectivity but is not necessarily focused on telecom networks. M2M is a part of IoT.

sa.q: State two differences between IoT and WoT.
sa.a: (1) IoT is about creating a network of objects, things, people, systems and applications; WoT tries to integrate them into the web using HTML5, JavaScript, Ajax, PHP and RESTful APIs. (2) WoT is a layer built on top of IoT, but IoT's scope is broader and includes systems not accessible through the web (conventional WSN, RFID).

sa.q: Differentiate structured and unstructured data.
sa.a: Structured data has a predefined structure, is associated with RDBMS, is created using length-limited fields (phone numbers, SSNs), is easily searchable, and is accessed using SQL. Unstructured data has no pre-defined structure, varies by application and source (text, email, video, images, sensor data, surveillance video), is very difficult to query, and uses NoSQL.

sa.q: Classify IoT data by urgency of processing with examples and time windows.
sa.a:
Very time critical — flight control, healthcare; a few milliseconds; processing requirements exceptionally high.
Time critical — vehicle, traffic, home automation, surveillance; a few seconds; allows transmission to remote locations or collaborative processing.
Normal — agriculture, environmental monitoring; a few minutes to hours; no particular urgency.

sa.q: Differentiate on-site and off-site processing.
sa.a:
On-site: data is processed at the source; for very time-critical applications with very low latency tolerance (healthcare, flight control); the infrastructure must be fast and robust.
Off-site: allows latencies and is significantly cheaper, because processing demands at the source are low; the sensor node only collects and frames data for transmission elsewhere.

sa.q: When would you use collaborative processing over remote processing?
sa.a: When there is limited or no network connectivity, or over large-scale deployments spread over vast areas where networked access to remote infrastructure is not viable. Nearby nodes club their processing power together. It also reduces latency from network transfer and conserves bandwidth. Agriculture is the classic case, since data is logged after long intervals.

sa.q: Differentiate FDMA and TDMA in the context of point-to-multipoint links.
sa.a: In point-to-multipoint connections the channel is shared either spatially — frequency division multiple access (FDMA), or temporally — time division multiple access (TDMA).

sa.q: Compare bus and ring topologies.
sa.a:
Bus: point-to-multipoint; a single cable acts as the backbone; hosts attach via drop lines/taps. Advantages: ease of installation, very low cable cost. Disadvantage: difficulty in fault localisation.
Ring: point-to-point; each node connects to exactly two others in a closed loop; packets travel around the ring to the destination. Advantages: ease of installation, low cable cost, ease of fault identification. Disadvantage: high probability of a single point of failure — one failed repeater downs the network.

sa.q: Compare LAN and WAN on three parameters.
sa.a: Scope: LAN covers a residence, lab, campus or office building; WAN connects diverse geographic locations (typically two LANs or MANs). Data rate: LAN is 100–1000 Mbps; WAN is a fraction of that. Fault tolerance / cost: LAN has very high fault tolerance; WAN has low fault tolerance, more errors and noise due to long ranges, and is very costly to maintain.

sa.q: State the PDU at each of the first four OSI layers.
sa.a: Physical → bits; Data link → frames; Network → packets; Transport → segments. (Session, presentation and application all use data.)

sa.q: Name the two data link sublayers and their functions.
sa.a: MAC (Medium Access Control) — access control and permissions for connecting networked devices. LLC (Logical Link Control) — error checking, flow control and frame synchronization.

sa.q: Compare TCP and UDP.
sa.a: TCP is connection-oriented; provides reliable, error-free communication; performs sequencing and segmentation; has acknowledgement and controls the flow of data. UDP is connectionless; provides no error-free guarantee and no acknowledgement; it is the go-to protocol and very cost-effective.

sa.q: Name the three Internet-layer protocols of TCP/IP and their jobs.
sa.a: IP — delivers packets from source to destination by looking at the IP addresses in packet headers. ICMP — provides hosts with information about network problems. ARP — finds the hardware address of a host from a known IP address.

sa.q: Define the five networking components of IoT.
sa.a: IoT node — connects to other nodes inside a LAN via the IoT LAN, sometimes directly to the Internet through a WAN. IoT gateway — a router connecting the IoT LAN to a WAN to the Internet, forwarding packets at the IP layer. IoT LAN — local, short-range connectivity, may or may not connect to the Internet. IoT WAN — connects network segments, few km to a hundred km, connects to the Internet. IoT proxy — performs active application layer functions between IoT nodes and other entities.

sa.q: How does gateway prefix allotment conserve addresses?
sa.a: Nodes use local addresses that exist uniquely only within the gateway's domain, so the same addresses can be repeated under a different gateway. Routers connected to the Internet assign prefixes to the gateways under them, giving each gateway a globally unique network prefix that identifies it. This saves a lot of unnecessary address wastage, at the cost that nodes must reach the Internet via the gateway.

sa.q: Give any four differences between IPv4 and IPv6.
sa.a: Length 32 vs 128 bits; dotted decimal vs hexadecimal; DHCP vs SLAAC/DHCPv6; IPSec optional vs compulsory; variable vs fixed header; checksum present vs absent; broadcast supported vs not supported. (Any four.)

sa.q: Explain the structure of an IPv6 address.
sa.a: 128 bits (16 bytes), written in hexadecimal, divided into 8 groups of 16 bits separated by colons. Structure: Global Routing Prefix (first 48 bits) identifies the organization; Subnet ID (next 16 bits) identifies a subnet within it; Interface ID (last 64 bits) identifies a host/interface on that subnet.

sa.q: How does ULA provide address stability under mobility?
sa.a: Mobility can change the network prefix, but the IoT LAN is unaffected because local addresses do not change with movement. With Unique Local Addresses, even if the gateway's WAN address changes the LAN addresses stay the same. Gateways are assigned prefixes and attached to a remote anchor point, making them immune to prefix changes. Where a node must reach the Internet directly, tunneling is used to send packets to the remote anchor point instead of routing through the gateway's router.

sa.q: What is multi-homing in IoT and what is its main challenge?
sa.a: In small IoT LANs where prefix allotment is not feasible, a proxy-based approach manages multiple IP addresses and maps them to link-local addresses; alternatively, IoT gateways with their own prefixes assign link-local addresses to their nodes. The real challenge is providing source addresses, destination addresses and routing information to multi-homed nodes. If source and destination addresses share a prefix, routing between gateways can be used for gateway selection.

sa.q: How does WirelessHART achieve deterministic, collision-free communication?
sa.a: The data link layer uses TDMA to avoid collisions, made deterministic with superframes — groups of 10 ms time slots that control transmission timing. Channel hopping increases reliability and security, and channel blacklisting removes channels consistently affected by interference. The Network Manager supervises each node, deciding who sends, who listens and at what frequency in each time slot.

sa.q: State the functions of the WirelessHART Network Manager.
sa.a: Supervises each node and guides them on when and where to send packets; allows collision-free and timely packet delivery; updates information about neighbours, signal strength and pending deliveries; decides who sends, who listens and at what frequency in each slot; handles code-based network security and prevents unauthorized nodes from joining.

sa.q: State four NFC specifications and its three modes of operation.
sa.a: Specifications: frequency 13.56 MHz; data rate 106/212/424 kbps; tag storage 96–512 bytes; range less than 20 cm. Modes: peer-to-peer (two NFC devices exchange information directly), read/write (an active device reads a passive device such as a tag), card emulation (the NFC device acts like a contactless smart card).

sa.q: Explain "Healing" in Z-Wave.
sa.a: Z-Wave uses a source-routed mesh. When devices are not in direct range, messages are routed through other nodes to bypass obstructions created by household appliances or layout. This process of bypassing radio dead spots is performed using a message called Healing.

sa.q: Why does LoRa operate below 1 GHz?
sa.a: LoRa uses unlicensed sub-GHz ISM bands (169, 433, 868, 915 MHz) because operating below 1 GHz gives better wall penetration and longer communication distance than 2.4 GHz technologies such as Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, with long range and low interference.

sa.q: Explain the working principle of RFID and its three components.
sa.a:
RFID uses tags and readers to communicate data without physical contact. Data is digitally encoded in the tag and read by the reader, then stored in a database. It is functionally similar to a barcode but needs no line of sight and can be read automatically over a distance.
Components: (1) RFID tag — an integrated circuit and an antenna, covered by protective material that also shields against environmental effects; passive tags are powered by the reader and are low cost and widely used, active tags have their own power source and can transmit without reader activation. (2) RFID reader — reads data from tags via radio waves and converts signals into a usable format. (3) Antenna — sends and receives radio waves between tag and reader.
Principle: RFID is derived from AIDC (Automatic Identification and Data Capture), which performs object identification, object data collection and mapping of that data to computer systems with little or no human intervention. AIDC uses wired communication; RFID performs AIDC functions using radio waves.

sa.q: Explain how Sigfox achieves excellent quality of service.
sa.a: Messages are transmitted using random access with time and frequency diversity. Base stations follow a cooperative reception principle — multiple base stations receive the same message, giving spatial diversity. The combination of time, frequency and spatial diversity ensures excellent QoS.
